item.title: How Do Husbands Feel About Wives With Higher Paying Jobs?
item.description:
Gender

How Do Husbands Feel About Wives With Higher Paying Jobs?

When salary disparity impacts marital satisfaction.

Posted August 9, 2026

Key points
  • Feelings about wives being the primary breadwinner differ between countries.
  • At home, men feel more satisfied when they provide emotional support to a working wife.
  • Women provide more emotional support to husbands, but benefit most when they receive it.

Traditionally, men were expected to be the financial providers for the family. Although that expectation has evolved over the years in many cultures, many people still hold expectations about which spouse should be the primary breadwinner, even within dual-income households.

Recent statistics show a decrease in working men and a rising number of working women,[1] sparking a renewed conversation about how dual-income couples can achieve a work-life blend, providing each other both financial and emotional support. Fortunately, research sheds some light on how dual-earning couples can maintain relational satisfaction at work and at home.

Source: Image by Pexels from Pixabay

Views About Breadwinning Wives

Even in modern times, some traditional attitudes persist when it comes to views about a woman’s contribution to the household. Sangsoo Lee (2025) explored the feeling of aversion to female breadwinning, defined as including marriages where wives outearn their husbands, studying individual attitudes towards women making more money in macro-level contexts.[2]

Lee found that on average, men experience more aversion to female breadwinning than women do, but within countries that have greater macro-level gender equality, both genders experience less aversion to female breadwinning. In countries with higher rates of unemployed men, he found a wider gender gap, with men experiencing a higher level of aversion, suggesting that men may react to economic uncertainty by overemphasizing their primary breadwinning role “to bolster their endangered masculinity.” Lee also found that in countries with more economic development, both genders feel less distaste for female breadwinning, which promotes a narrower gender gap.

Compounding the daily grind of a work schedule is the stress of having bad days at work, highlighting the importance of spousal emotional support at home. Here too, there are differences in the way husbands and wives prefer to give and receive support.

Spousal Support: From Economic to Emotional

When both spouses are working, husbands and wives still desire personal support from each other, particularly after a difficult day in the workplace. Gender roles matter here too, with men and women feeling emotionally satisfied in different ways.

Helen Pluut et al. (2025) in “The Things I Do for You” explored the way husbands and wives in dual-earning marriages support each other emotionally.[3] They began by acknowledging that historically, men were viewed as the financial providers and women were homemakers, depending on a husband’s income to support the family. As dual-earner families have become more common, traditional roles have become outdated in many parts of the world. Yet Pluut et al. recognize a similar asymmetry within the area of social/emotional support as a result of heavy work demands faced by dual-earner couples. On days characterized by “work-to-family conflict,” when one spouse feels emotionally exhausted due to work demands, Pluut et al. found that wives are more inclined to increase support to their husbands, not the other way around. In fact, they found that husbands actually decreased emotional support on days when wives experienced work-family conflict, even though wives offered higher levels of social support on days where husbands reported more emotional exhaustion.

Pluut et al. acknowledge that both partners benefit from both providing and receiving support, although men benefit most when they provide support, and women benefit most when they receive it, consistent with traditional gender norms. They also found that only women were more satisfied with their relationship when their husband offered social support, and only men felt more life satisfaction when they provided spousal support to their wives. Pluut et al. note their results demonstrate that social support benefits depend not only on gender, but also on whether husbands and wives were the provider or receiver of spousal support.

Working couples are wise to recognize and implement how they can provide for the family both economically and emotionally, to maintain relational satisfaction and marital quality.
